title: Travel Restrictions: Reachability Along a Directed Path
sourceTitle: Facebook Hacker Cup 2020, Qualification Round — Travel Restrictions
sourceNote: Public Hacker Cup contest problem, preserved in the organizer-released HackerCupAI archive.
prompt: N countries form a line, with flights only between adjacent countries. A flight u → v is allowed exactly when outgoing[u] and incoming[v] are both Y. For 2 ≤ N ≤ 50, return the N × N reachability matrix, including zero-flight trips.
approach: For each start s, mark s reachable. Scan right while each consecutive directed flight is allowed, stopping at the first blocked edge.
Scan left under the same rule, using the departure country’s outgoing flag and the arrival country’s incoming flag.
The reachable destinations form one interval containing s: every route to a farther country must cross each intervening edge. Fill that interval with Y and other entries with N.
complexity: O(N²) time, which matches the output size; O(1) auxiliary space when rows are streamed, or O(N²) space for the returned matrix.
pitfalls: Restrictions are directional; the return trip may fail.
A country always reaches itself, even when both flags are N.
followUp: Answer individual reachability queries after preprocessing blocked-edge prefix counts.
answer: incoming = NY and outgoing = YY yield rows YY and NY: country 1 reaches 2, while country 2 cannot enter 1.

examples.explanation: Entering the first country is blocked.
Only zero-flight trips remain possible.

title: Timber: Join Two Sparse Endpoint Dynamic Programs
sourceTitle: Facebook Hacker Cup 2020, Qualification Round — Timber
sourceNote: Public Hacker Cup contest problem, preserved in the organizer-released HackerCupAI archive.
prompt: Each tree has a distinct integer position P and positive height H. Fell it left to [P − H, P], right to [P, P + H], or leave it standing. Felled intervals may touch but cannot overlap with positive length. Maximize the length of one connected timber interval; N can reach 800,000.
approach: Sort trees by position. Let R[x] be the longest connected chain ending at x using only right-falling trees. Update R[P + H] = max(R[P + H], R[P] + H). Missing entries are zero.
Traverse in reverse. Let L[x] be the longest left-falling chain starting at x. Update L[P − H] = max(L[P − H], L[P] + H).
Return max_x(R[x] + L[x]). A connected chain has right-falling trees followed by left-falling trees; their base positions lie on opposite sides of the joining point, so no tree is reused.
complexity: O(N log N) time and O(N) space with sorting and balanced maps; hash maps give the same expected time bound.
pitfalls: Overlapping standing trees are permitted; overlapping felled intervals are not.
Do not combine both orientations of the same tree.
followUp: Store predecessor choices and recover the chosen trees and directions.
answer: Trees (0, 5) and (9, 4) attain length 9 by falling right and left, meeting at coordinate 5.

examples.explanation: Intervals [0, 5] and [5, 9] touch.
One tree contributes only once, regardless of direction.

title: Consistency, Chapter 2: Shortest Character Conversions
sourceTitle: Facebook Hacker Cup 2021, Qualification Round — Consistency, Chapter 2
sourceNote: Public Hacker Cup contest problem, preserved in the organizer-released HackerCupAI archive.
prompt: Given a nonempty uppercase string S and up to 300 directed character-replacement rules, replace one occurrence per second. Rules may be reused and chained. Minimize the seconds needed to make every character identical, or return −1 if impossible. The original bound is |S| ≤ 100.
approach: Build a 26-letter directed graph with unit-cost rule edges, zero diagonal distances, and infinity for other pairs.
Run Floyd–Warshall with intermediate letter k outermost: d[a][b] = min(d[a][b], d[a][k] + d[k][b]).
Count character frequencies. For each target t, sum frequency[a] × d[a][t]; reject targets unreachable from any present character. Return the smallest finite sum, or −1.
complexity: For alphabet size A and K rules, O(|S| + K + A³) time and O(A²) space; here A = 26.
pitfalls: A → B does not imply B → A.
A valid target need not already appear in the string.
followUp: Replace Floyd–Warshall with one BFS per source letter and compare the bounds.
answer: For S = AC and rules A → B, B → C, converting A through B to C costs 2 seconds.

examples.explanation: Convert the A occurrence twice; C stays unchanged.
B and C have no shared reachable target.
The string is already consistent.

title: Xs and Os: Count Distinct Winning Move Sets
sourceTitle: Facebook Hacker Cup 2021, Qualification Round — Xs and Os
sourceNote: Public Hacker Cup contest problem, preserved in the organizer-released HackerCupAI archive.
prompt: An N × N board contains X, O, and empty cells, with equal X/O counts and no winner yet; 2 ≤ N ≤ 50. Add Xs without an opponent move. Find the fewest additions that complete a row or column, and count distinct optimal cell sets. Diagonals do not win. Report Impossible if none exists.
approach: Discard every row or column containing O. Count the empty cells in each remaining line; the minimum count m is the minimum required additions.
If m ≥ 2, count the lines attaining m: different rows are disjoint, and a row and column intersect in at most one cell, so their move sets cannot coincide.
If m = 1, deduplicate the single empty-cell coordinates with a set. One placement may complete both a row and a column. If no eligible line exists, report Impossible.
complexity: O(N²) time and O(N) auxiliary space beyond the input board.
pitfalls: Count sets of placements, not winning lines.
Do not include diagonals or model alternating turns.
followUp: Generalize the rules to additional winning shapes and use canonical cell-set keys.
answer: On [OXO, X.X, OXO], filling the center completes both its row and column: the answer is 1 move and 1 distinct set.

examples.explanation: The two winning lines require the same center cell.
Each of three rows and three columns gives a different set.
Every row and column contains an O.

title: Weak Typing, Chapter 2: Count Each Forced Switch’s Contribution
sourceTitle: Facebook Hacker Cup 2021, Round 1 — Weak Typing, Chapter 2
sourceNote: Public Hacker Cup contest problem, preserved in the organizer-released HackerCupAI archive.
prompt: For a string over X, O, F, X requires the left hand, O the right, and F either. A substring may start with either hand. Sum its minimum required hand switches over all substring occurrences, modulo 1,000,000,007. The original length bound is 800,000.
approach: Ignore F when identifying required hands, but retain original indices. A forced switch occurs between consecutive non-F characters of different types.
For such a pair at zero-based indices a < b, exactly (a + 1)(N − b) substrings contain both endpoints. Add this contribution modulo the modulus.
Scan once, tracking the last non-F character and its position. Every substring’s switches are counted once per consecutive opposite-hand pair inside it.
complexity: O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space for a supplied string of length N.
pitfalls: Deleting F before computing positions gives incorrect substring counts.
Use wide integer products before reducing modulo 1,000,000,007.
followUp: Derive a streaming recurrence that does not need N until the final character arrives.
answer: For XOX, the two switch pairs each contribute 2, so the total is 4.

examples.explanation: Only the full substring requires a hand switch.
XO and OX contribute 1 each; XOX contributes 2.
The switch-pair contributions are 5 × 4 and 8 × 2, totaling 36.

title: Second Second Friend: Preserve Required Vertices in a Graph’s 2-core
sourceTitle: Meta Hacker Cup 2022, Qualification Round — Second Second Friend
sourceNote: Public Hacker Cup contest problem, preserved in the organizer-released HackerCupAI archive.
prompt: A rectangular grid contains empty cells, trees (^), and rocks (#). Add trees only in empty cells so every final tree has at least two orthogonally adjacent trees. Preserve existing trees and rocks. Return any valid grid, or Impossible. Rows and columns can each reach 3,000.
approach: Treat non-rock cells as vertices with orthogonal edges. Initially consider all of them possible tree locations and compute their degrees.
Queue vertices of degree below 2. Remove each once, decrement surviving neighbors’ degrees, and queue newly deficient neighbors. These vertices cannot occur in any valid final tree set.
The survivors form the graph’s 2-core. If an original tree was removed, return Impossible. Otherwise fill every survivor with a tree and leave other non-rock cells empty.
complexity: O(RC) time and O(RC) auxiliary space; each cell and adjacency is processed a constant number of times.
pitfalls: A removed leaf can trigger further removals.
An empty final tree set is valid when there were no required trees.
followUp: Generalize to at least k neighbors and explain why the surviving core is independent of removal order.
answer: On [^.#, ..#], the four non-rock cells form a cycle. Filling them yields [^^#, ^^#].

examples.explanation: All four trees have exactly two tree neighbors.
A path has no nonempty 2-core.
With no required tree, leaving the grid unchanged is valid.

title: Watering Well, Chapter 1: Replace Pairwise Distances with Moments
sourceTitle: Meta Hacker Cup 2022, Round 1 — Watering Well, Chapter 1
sourceNote: Public Hacker Cup contest problem, preserved in the organizer-released HackerCupAI archive.
prompt: Given N tree coordinates and Q candidate wells, return the sum of squared Euclidean distances over all tree–well pairs, modulo 1,000,000,007. Each set contains distinct points; 1 ≤ N,Q ≤ 500,000 and coordinates lie in [0,3000].
approach: Stream trees into three summaries: Sx = ΣA_i, Sy = ΣB_i, and S2 = Σ(A_i² + B_i²), retaining their count N.
For a well (x,y), expand the squares: cost = N(x² + y²) − 2xSx − 2ySy + S2. This equals the sum of its squared distances to all trees.
Add each well’s cost modulo 1,000,000,007, normalizing negative residues. Use exact wide integer multiplication or BigInt before modular reduction.
complexity: O(N + Q) time and O(1) auxiliary space with streamed coordinates and fixed-width exact arithmetic under the original bounds.
pitfalls: Squared Euclidean distance is not the unsquared distance.
JavaScript Number cannot safely represent every unreduced total; reduce regularly or use exact integers.
followUp: Support weighted trees or dynamic insertions by updating the same summaries.

examples.explanation: Summing the four squared distances gives 9 + 9 + 32 + 2.
Each tree contributes squared distance 1.

title: Ready, Go, Part 2: Aggregate Groups Sharing One Liberty
sourceTitle: Meta Hacker Cup 2023, Round 2 — Ready, Go, Part 2
sourceNote: Public Hacker Cup contest problem, preserved in the organizer-released HackerCupAI archive.
prompt: A valid Go board contains black stones B, white stones W, and empty cells; every existing group has at least one adjacent empty cell. Groups use orthogonal connectivity. Place one black stone to capture as many white stones as possible. A group is captured when it loses its last adjacent empty cell. Return the maximum count; dimensions can reach 3,000.
approach: Flood-fill each white group once. Count its stones and collect its distinct adjacent empty cells, called liberties.
A group is capturable in one move exactly when it has one distinct liberty. Add its size to a score indexed by that cell; several groups may contribute to the same move.
Return the largest cell score, or 0 if no group can be captured. An iterative traversal avoids recursive-stack failure on large groups.
complexity: O(RC) time and O(RC) auxiliary space. There are at most four adjacency checks per cell.
pitfalls: Count distinct liberty cells, not white-to-empty boundary edges.
Taking the largest single group misses simultaneous captures.
followUp: Retain a maximizing move and the captured groups; cap each temporary liberty set at two distinct cells.
answer: For [W..., B.BB, .BWW, .BW.], playing at the bottom-right empty cell captures the connected group of 3 white stones.

examples.explanation: The bottom-right white group has one distinct liberty, touched by two of its stones.
The center move captures two white groups of size 2 each.
There are no white stones to capture.
